title: The one whose head He guards
hookLine: the one who has You over his head, how can he suffer (Suhi M5, ang 749)

lines: A CHILD TOUCHES AN ELDER'S FEET.
A HAND RESTS ON THE HEAD.
cards: In Punjabi homes, when a child bends to touch a grandparent's feet, the grandparent often rests a hand on the child's head, without thinking. A second, maybe two. It means: I bless you, I've got you, you're under my care.
There's even an everyday phrase for having someone's hand on your head: you have a protector, someone who stands behind you. Guru Arjan took that gesture and lifted it as high as it can go.

teach.h: SIR: THE HEAD, WHERE BLESSING LANDS.
teach.b: The shabad is in Raag Suhi, on ang 749.

teach.h: HOW COULD SUCH A ONE SUFFER?
teach.b: It begins, in effect: the one over whose head You stand, my Master, how could such a one suffer?

Then the opposite person: someone drunk on the world's glitter doesn't know how to speak, and never remembers that he will die. Then the refrain: my Sovereign, You belong to Your devoted ones, and they belong to You.

Your servant has no fear; even death's messenger doesn't come near. The word in the first line is sir, head, where blessing lands and protection is felt. Now the honest question, the one we asked about You are my father.
Does this mean nothing bad ever happens to the faithful?

Guru Arjan answers that with his life. In 1606 he was arrested by the Mughal authorities in Lahore and died in their custody, after suffering Sikhs remember with grief every year. He's honored as the first Sikh martyr.
So the hymn can't mean his devoted ones never meet pain. Sikhs read it at a deeper level: the one under the Master's hand isn't crushed by suffering.

teach.h: PAIN COMES, BUT DOESN'T OWN THEM.
teach.b: Dukh, pain, can come, but it doesn't own them. The fear is gone, even when the danger isn't. Tradition remembers Guru Arjan in his last days repeating that the Lord's will is sweet.
That's a guarded head: not a life without storms, but a person who stays steady inside one.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Suhi shabad 'jis ke sir oopar toon suaamee' in kirtan, especially in hard times, and remember his martyrdom in 1606 each year.

o: pride, the ego held up high
a crown, a sign of earthly power

games.q: the guarded head — tap the pairs.

s: the hymn means the faithful never meet pain
Guru Arjan himself was martyred; Sikhs read it as freedom from fear, not from storms.
Guru Arjan is honored as the first Sikh martyr
he died in Mughal custody in Lahore in 1606.
the refrain says the Lord belongs to His devoted ones

games.q: Guru Arjan wrote that the one under the Master's hand cannot suffer. then he was arrested and tortured. what does tradition remember him saying?
o: that the Lord's will is sweet.
games.why: pain came, but did not own him: a guarded head is a steady one, not a sheltered one.

practice: Rest your hand gently on your head, the way a grandparent would, let your shoulders drop under its weight and warmth, and think of who has been that hand for you: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend.
Then bring to mind something you're afraid of, and hold the fear and the hand at the same time. If you pray, let the hand stand for the One's, and say Waheguru quietly.

wordCard.voice: Sir, head, where blessing lands: Guru Arjan says the one with the Master's hand over it may meet pain, but not fear.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: head; jis ke sir oopar, the one over whose head You stand.

carryVoice: Your line: guarded. Not spared every storm, but steady inside each one. See you tomorrow, then.

sources.ref: Suhi M5, Ang 749 (jis ke sir oopar toon suaamee)
